content: 1. Do not share any confidential information about clients with other providers or outside the health facility. 2. Arrange the examination area to ensure the woman is shielded from the view of others during the examination. Use curtains, screens, or walls to maintain privacy. 3. Keep all medical records confidential and securely locked away. 4. When prescribing or administering treatments (e.g., drugs, vaccines, bed nets, condoms) at the clinic or recommending measures for home use: Clearly explain the treatment to the woman, including its purpose and necessity. Reassure her that the treatment will not harm her or her baby, and emphasize that avoiding the treatment may pose greater risks. Provide detailed instructions on how to take the medication regularly. For example: Take two tablets three times a day, every eight hours (morning, afternoon, and evening) with water and after meals, for five days. Demonstrate the procedure if necessary. Explain how the treatment should be administered to the baby. Discuss potential side effects, emphasizing that they are not serious, and provide guidance on how to manage them. Advise her to return to the clinic if she experiences any problems or concerns with the medication. Explore any barriers she or her family may have regarding the treatment, such as prior experiences or misinformation, and address these concerns by reinforcing accurate information. 5. Discuss the importance of purchasing and taking the prescribed amount of medication. 6. Ensure service hours are clearly posted at the workplace. 7. Be punctual for appointments or inform the woman if there will be a delay. 8. Before starting services, verify that all equipment is clean, functional, and that supplies and medications are available. 9. Maintain cleanliness in the facility through regular cleaning. 10. At the end of the service: Safely dispose of waste and sharps. Prepare equipment and supplies for disinfection. Replace linens and prepare them for washing. Replenish supplies and medications. Ensure routine cleaning of all areas. 11. Keep records of equipment, supplies, medications, and vaccines. Regularly check their availability and functionality, and reorder stocks before they run out. 12. Establish staff schedules and maintain staffing lists. 13. Always document clinical findings, treatments, reasons for referrals, and follow-up recommendations in the clinical record at the time of observation. 14. Do not record confidential information in the home-based record if the woman is unwilling. 15. The health facility must not distribute free or low-cost supplies or products that violate the International Code of Marketing of Breast Milk Substitutes. 16. Follow standard precautions to protect the woman, her baby, and yourself from infections, including HIV: Wash hands with soap and water before and after caring for a woman or newborn, before any treatment procedure, after contamination with blood or body fluids, after removing gloves, and after handling soiled linens or clothing. Keep nails short. Wear sterile gloves for vaginal examinations, deliveries, cord cutting, episiotomy repair, or blood drawing. Use long sterile gloves for manual removal of the placenta. Wear clean gloves when handling and cleaning instruments, contaminated waste, or cleaning blood and body fluid spills. Protect yourself from blood and body fluids during deliveries by wearing gloves, covering cuts or abrasions with waterproof bandages, using good lighting, and practicing safe sharps disposal. Wear a long plastic or fluid-resistant apron, shoes, and protect your eyes and mouth from splashes. 17. Practice safe sharps disposal: Keep a puncture-resistant container nearby. Use each needle and syringe only once. Do not recap, bend, or break needles after use. Dispose of them directly into the container without passing them to another person. 18. Dispose of waste safely: Place contaminated items in leak-proof containers. Burn or bury solid waste. Wash hands, gloves, and containers after disposing of infectious waste. Pour liquid waste down a drain or flushable toilet. 19. Handle contaminated laundry carefully: Collect bloodor body fluid-stained clothing or sheets separately, wearing gloves or using a plastic bag. Do not touch them directly. Rinse off blood or body fluids before washing with soap. 20. Sterilize and clean contaminated equipment: Ensure instruments that penetrate the skin (e.g., needles) are sterilized or disposed of after one use. Thoroughly clean or disinfect equipment that contacts intact skin according to instructions. 21. Reusing gloves is not recommended. If necessary due to limited supply, clean and disinfect them: Wash gloves with soap and water. Check for damage by inflating them with air and submerging them in clean water to look for leaks. Discard if damaged. Disinfect with a 5% chlorine solution, dry away from direct sunlight, and dust the inside with talcum powder or starch. Note that disinfected gloves are not sterile. 22. When organizing a visit: Greet the woman and offer her a seat. Introduce yourself and ask for her name (and the baby’s name, if applicable). Ask why she came (e.g., for herself, her baby, a routine visit, or specific complaints). Determine if it is a first or follow-up visit and whether she wants a companion or family member involved. If the woman recently delivered, assess the baby or ask to see the baby if not present. For antenatal care, revise the birth plan at the end of the visit. For postpartum visits, examine the baby if present and follow the appropriate charts based on pregnancy status, baby’s age, and visit purpose. 23. During the visit: Explain all procedures and ask for permission before conducting examinations or tests. Keep the woman informed throughout and discuss findings with her (and her partner, if applicable). Ensure privacy during examinations and discussions. 24. At the end of the visit: Ask if the woman has any questions. Summarize the most important messages with her. Encourage her to return for routine visits and inform her when to come back or if she has any concerns. Complete the Home-Based Maternal Record (HBMR) and provide her with the appropriate information sheet.
